{{Short description|Equation in fluid dynamics}}
{{for|the superconductivity theory|Ginzburg–Landau theory}}
The '''Ginzburg–Landau equation''', named after [[Vitaly Ginzburg]] and [[Lev Landau]], describes the nonlinear evolution of small disturbances near a finite wavelength [[bifurcation theory|bifurcation]] from a stable to an unstable state of a system. At the onset of finite wavelength bifurcation, the system becomes unstable for a critical wavenumber <math>k_c</math> which is non-zero. In the neighbourhood of this bifurcation, the evolution of disturbances is characterised by the particular Fourier mode for <math>k_c</math> with slowly varying amplitude <math>A</math> (more precisely the real part of <math>A</math>). The Ginzburg–Landau equation is the governing equation for <math>A</math>. The unstable modes can either be non-oscillatory (stationary) or oscillatory.<ref>Cross, M. C., & Hohenberg, P. C. (1993). Pattern formation outside of equilibrium. Reviews of modern physics, 65(3), 851.</ref><ref>Cross, M., & Greenside, H. (2009). Pattern formation and dynamics in nonequilibrium systems. Cambridge University Press.</ref>

For non-oscillatory bifurcation, <math>A</math> satisfies the '''real Ginzburg–Landau equation'''

:<math>\frac{\partial A}{\partial t} = \nabla^2 A + A - A|A|^2</math>

which was first derived by [[Alan C. Newell]] and John A. Whitehead<ref>Newell, A. C., & Whitehead, J. A. (1969). Finite bandwidth, finite amplitude convection. Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 38(2), 279-303.</ref> and by [[Lee Segel]]<ref>Segel, L. A. (1969). Distant side-walls cause slow amplitude modulation of cellular convection. Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 38(1), 203-224.</ref> in 1969. For oscillatory bifurcation, <math>A</math> satisfies the '''complex Ginzburg–Landau equation'''

:<math>\frac{\partial A}{\partial t} = (1+i\alpha)\nabla^2 A + A - (1+i\beta) A|A|^2</math>

which was first derived by [[Keith Stewartson]] and [[John Trevor Stuart]] in 1971.<ref>Stewartson, K., & Stuart, J. T. (1971). A non-linear instability theory for a wave system in plane Poiseuille flow. Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 48(3), 529-545.</ref> Here <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> are real constants.

When the problem is homogeneous, i.e., when <math>A</math> is independent of the spatial coordinates, the Ginzburg–Landau equation reduces to [[Stuart–Landau equation]]. The [[Swift–Hohenberg equation]] results in the Ginzburg–Landau equation.

Substituting <math>A(\mathbf x,t) = Re^{i\Theta}</math>, where <math>R=|A|</math> is the amplitude and <math>\Theta=\mathrm{arg}(A)</math> is the phase, one obtains the following equations

:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{\partial R}{\partial t} &= [\nabla^2 R - R (\nabla \Theta)^2] - \alpha(2\nabla\Theta\cdot\nabla R + R \nabla^2\Theta) + (1-R^2)R,\\
R\frac{\partial \Theta}{\partial t} & = \alpha[\nabla^2 R - R (\nabla \Theta)^2] + (2\nabla\Theta\cdot\nabla R + R \nabla^2\Theta) - \beta R^3.
\end{align}</math>

==Some solutions of the real Ginzburg–Landau equation==

===Steady plane-wave type===
If we substitute <math>A = f(k) e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}</math> in the real equation without the [[time derivative]] term, we obtain

:<math>A(\mathbf x) = \sqrt{1-k^2} e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}, \quad |k|<1.</math>

This solution is known to become unstable due to Eckhaus instability for wavenumbers <math>k^2>1/3.</math>

===Steady solution with absorbing boundary condition===
Once again, let us look for steady solutions, but with an [[absorbing boundary condition]] <math>A=0</math> at some location. In a semi-infinite, 1D domain <math>0\leq x< \infty</math>, the solution is given by

:<math>A(x) = e^{ia} \tanh \frac{x}{\sqrt 2},</math>

where <math>a</math> is an arbitrary real constant. Similar solutions can be constructed numerically in a finite domain.

==Some solutions of the complex Ginzburg–Landau equation==

===Traveling wave===
The traveling wave solution is given by

:<math>A(\mathbf x,t) = \sqrt{1-k^2} e^{i\mathbf k\cdot \mathbf x-i\omega t}, \quad \omega = \beta + (\alpha-\beta) k^2, \quad |k|<1.</math>

The [[group velocity]] of the wave is given by <math>d\omega/dk = 2(\alpha-\beta)k.</math> The above solution becomes unstable due to [[Benjamin–Feir instability]] for wavenumbers <math>k^2>(1+\alpha\beta)/(2\beta^2+\alpha\beta+3).</math>

===Hocking–Stewartson pulse===
Hocking–Stewartson pulse refers to a quasi-steady, 1D solution of the complex Ginzburg–Landau equation, obtained by Leslie M. Hocking and [[Keith Stewartson]] in 1972.<ref>Hocking, L. M., & Stewartson, K. (1972). On the nonlinear response of a marginally unstable plane parallel flow to a two-dimensional disturbance. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. A. Mathematical and Physical Sciences, 326(1566), 289-313.</ref> The solution is given by

:<math>A(x,t) = \lambda L e^{i\nu t}(\mathrm{sech} \lambda x)^{1+iM}</math>

where the four real constants in the above solution satisfy

:<math>\lambda^2(M^2+2\alpha-1) =1, \quad \lambda^2(\alpha-\alpha M^2+2M) =\nu,</math>
:<math>2-M^2-3\alpha M = -L^2, \quad 2\alpha+3M-\alpha M^2 = -\beta L^2.</math>

===Coherent structure solutions===
The coherent structure solutions are obtained by assuming <math>A= e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t}B(\boldsymbol \xi,t)</math> where <math>\boldsymbol\xi=\mathbf x+\mathbf u t</math>. This leads to

:<math>\frac{\partial B}{\partial t} + \mathbf v \cdot \nabla B = (1+i\alpha ) \nabla^2 B + \lambda B - (1+i\beta) B|B|^2</math>

where <math>\mathbf v = \mathbf u + (1+i\alpha) \mathbf k</math> and <math>\lambda = 1+i\omega-(1+i\alpha)k^2.</math>
